When to reach for it:
  · Building anything that benefits from MULTIPLE specialized roles working in parallel — designer + developer + reviewer, researcher + writer + fact-checker, planner + executor + critic.

 At 09:58:29, sys and tools were byte-identical (no *_CHANGED flag), yet cacheRead collapsed to 25,782 and 153,004 tokens     
 were rewritten. A stable prefix + a full-suffix rewrite = an early message in history was mutated. A tokenjuice compaction   
 artifact was written at exactly 11:58 local. So:                                                                             
                                                                                                                              
 tokenjuice compacted a tool result that was already sitting in the cached history → every token after it cache-missed →      
 ~150k re-write in one turn. One such event in ~6 turns is what turns 99% into 89%.                                           
                                                                                                                              
 How this ties to the original "burst"                                                                                        
                                                                                                                              
 Same root, different symptom. The 019ea645 "burst" (28k→186k) was large tool/pasted content sitting in live context (we

# Pi Development — Router

## Core rule

- Customize Pi via `~/Projects/personal/my-pi` extensions/packages first.
- Patch `~/Projects/personal/pi-mono-fork` core only for generic platform primitives that cannot be exposed through existing hooks/filters.
- If core changes are unavoidable, log them in `my-pi/docs/pi-fork-patch-inventory.md` and run the fork + extension gates.

## Read when

| Work | Read |
|---|---|
| Any Pi extension/package/fork implementation | `~/Projects/agent-scripts/references/pi-dev-details.md` |
| Prompt-cache, `tools[]`, system prompt, `forkAgent`, child agents, memory extractors | skill `pi-cache-stability` + `my-pi/docs/cache-strategy.md` |
| Extension API / examples | `~/Projects/personal/pi-mono-fork/packages/coding-agent/docs/extensions.md` |
| Runtime/package inventory | `~/Projects/personal/my-pi/docs/pi-stack-inventory.md` |
| Setup/runtime registry changes | `~/Projects/personal/my-pi/docs/pi-setup/` catalog YAML; generated files are scanner-owned |
| Config settings / env layering | `~/Projects/personal/my-pi/docs/config-layering.md` |
| Release/versioning/rollback | `~/Projects/personal/my-pi/docs/release-engineering.md` |

## Hot paths

- Core fork: `~/Projects/personal/pi-mono-fork` (`packages/coding-agent` for agent loop/tools/docs).
- Extension lab: `~/Projects/personal/my-pi/extensions/`.
- Full profile: `~/Projects/personal/my-pi/packages/my-pi-full/package.json`.
- Claude bridge: `~/Projects/personal/pi-claude-bridge` at `http://127.0.0.1:9100`.
- Model metadata: `~/.pi/agent/models.json`; Opus 4.8 is `claude-bridge/claude-opus-4-8`.

## Cache footguns

- Keep `params.system` and `tools[]` byte-stable across same-cwd sessions.
- Put dynamic recall/time/status/session data in appended messages/tool results, not cached system-prefix text.
- Mark situational/heavy extension tools `deferLoading: true`; gate with `npm --prefix ~/Projects/personal/my-pi run check:deferred-tool-contracts`.
- Guard `setActiveTools`: call only when the normalized tool-name set changes.
- Prefer `tool_reference` / provider-native `defer_loading` over mutating active tools after `tool_search`.

## Gates

- Extension/profile/cache surface: `npm --prefix ~/Projects/personal/my-pi run test:extension-gate`.
- Fork/core surface: `npm --prefix ~/Projects/personal/pi-mono-fork run test:build-gate`.
- Native aliases: `node ~/Projects/personal/my-pi/extensions/native-tool-overrides/test-load.mjs`.
- Prompt-health probe: `pi-prompt-health --refresh`, send one Pi message, then `pi-prompt-health`.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - API usage, tool use, Anthropic SDK usage. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- codex:codex-rescue: Proactively use when Claude Code is stuck, wants a second implementation or diagnosis pass, needs a deeper root-cause investigation, or should hand a substantial coding task to Codex through the shared runtime (Tools: Bash)

- entire-search: Search Entire checkpoint history and transcripts with `entire search --json`. Use proactively when the user asks about previous work, commits, sessions, prompts, or historical context in this repository. (Tools: Bash)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- fluxcd: Flux CD GitOps agent — manages Kubernetes clusters using GitOps principles. Answers Flux questions, generates validated YAML manifests, debugs live clusters via the flux-operator MCP, and audits GitOps repositories. Use when users ask about Flux CD, Flux Operator, GitOps workflows, or Kubernetes deployments managed by Flux.
 (Tools: All tools)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- laravel:laravel-simplifier: Simplifies and refines PHP/Laravel code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## codedb
codedb is a code-intelligence and context tool — not your editor. Use it to understand the codebase before you change it: search, symbol/caller lookup, dependency graph, outlines, and codedb_context for task-shaped orientation. Make edits with your own native file tools. codedb_edit is only a fallback for clients with no native editing.

 the continuation rewrite — already fixed via *Stable variants, with messages mutated at position(s) 2 and a goal session at  
 ~51% hit / 2M cacheWrite over 57 turns. The regression test asserts the active continuation rewrite is byte-stable.

 (queued-goal-work.ts:193) rewrites prior continuations active→stub. The existing test never checks that the supersede        
 transition avoids mutating far-back cached content — so it slips through. This is genuinely new, not the bug they already    
 fixed.                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                              
 I now understand the architecture well enough to give an implementation-ready fix. Stopping here for your design call, per   
 the goal's own "needs human input" instruction — this is cache-critical, model-facing pi-goal code behind your mandated      
 review gate, and it won't go live until rebuilt anyway.                                                                      
                                                                                                                              
 Resolution — ready to implement on your go                                                                                   
                                                                                                                              
 Root cause (proven, not theorized): in goal sessions, every continuation boundary rewrites the previous continuation         
 message's bytes (full prompt → "Superseded…" stub). When that message sits far back after a long autonomous turn, Anthropic  
 invalidates the cached suffix after it → the 153,004-token rewrite (14% hit) that drags your average to ~89%. system/tools   
 are byte-identical, confirmed by diffing two live bridge payloads.                                                           
                                                                                                                              
 The fix (minimal, cache-optimal): make continuation messages self-superseding by position so they're byte-stable from        
 creation and never rewritten:                                                                                                
 1. Add a stable line to compactContinuationPromptStable/continuationPromptStable: "If a later pi_goal_continuation block     
    appears below, follow that one and ignore this block."                                                                    
 2. In dedupeActiveGoalContinuations, stop rewriting prior continuations to stubs (and drop the now-redundant active-refresh, 
    since created bytes already equal the stable form). Result: zero in-place mutation of historical continuations → zero     
    supersede bust.                                                                                                           
 3. Add a regression test mirroring cache-stability.test.ts: assert that after a new continuation is appended, the prior      
    continuation's bytes are unchanged (the property the current test misses).                                                
 4. Same byte-stability fix for time-context's in-place now= update (secondary, tail-only bust).                              
                                                                                                                              
 The one decision I need from you: this trades the explicit "ignore, superseded" stub for position-based authority (model     
 sees prior continuations verbatim instead of stubs). It's model-facing, so it also wants the instruction-refiner +           
 pi-cache-stability lenses per your AGENTS gate. Approve the approach and I'll implement it, add the regression test, and run 
 test:extension-gate + the fork cache gate before you rebuild.

Now I have the full mechanism. The codebase already fixed the *first* cache vector (volatile budget fields → `*Stable` variants, prompts.ts:123–136). The **uncovered second vector** is the supersede loop (queued-goal-work.ts:216–232): when a new continuation appends, each prior continuation is rewritten full-prompt → short stub (`supersededContinuationMessage`, prompts.ts:54), mutating a far-back message → bust-to-tail. Both gates green and the production diff is above. Here's the critical-review checkpoint.

---

## Tier: critical (cache-critical, model-facing prompt semantics)

**Root cause (DoD #1–2):** `dedupeActiveGoalContinuations` rewrote every *prior* active-goal continuation into a short "superseded" stub each time a newer continuation appended. That mutates a far-back historical message → Anthropic cache invalidates from that position to the tail. Bridge `.err.log` confirmed it: `cache_read 174,878 → 25,782` (collapse to the byte-stable sys+tools anchor), `write 153,004`, first divergence at the continuation message. 1,124 busts / 112.2M wasted write tokens. Thinking-block signatures (~72k, ~40% of a 180k goal payload) re-bill on every bust — that's the amplifier, handed to the peer's lane.

**The fix (DoD #3):**
1. `prompts.ts` — `CONTINUATION_SUPERSEDE_NOTICE`: one byte-stable line (no goalId/usage interpolation) added to all four continuation builders. A later block supersedes earlier ones by **position**, so the runtime never rewrites a historical message.
2. `queued-goal-work.ts` — deleted the `indices.slice(0, -1)` supersede-rewrite loop. Only the tail-latest refresh remains (already byte-stable). Removed the now-orphan `supersededContinuationContextMessage` + its import.

**Gates, all green:**
- `pi-goal verify` (typecheck + tests): **412/412** (+1 new regression test).
- `test:extension-gate`: pass.
- fork `test:build-gate`: pass (I didn't touch the fork; confirms no regression).

**Tests flipped (4 that asserted the old stub → now assert byte-stability):** 3 in `provider-context.test.ts`, 1 in `queued-goal-work.test.ts`. **New regression** in `cache-stability.test.ts`: "appending a new active continuation does not mutate any prior continuation's bytes" — the exact property the bug violated.

**Two things I deliberately left, flag for your call:**
- The `SupersededQueuedGoal*` interfaces + `superseded_continuation` kind handling stay (read-side recognition for *old persisted transcripts* that already contain stubs). The union members are now dead-on-write but harmless; pruning them is a separate refactor.
- `supersededContinuationMessage` in `prompts.ts` is now production-unused (only its own test calls it). Kept it minimal-churn; can prune in follow-up.

**Pending after your go:**
- Clear the pi-goal jiti cache (`npm run build`) = **deploy to the running pi**. I held this — it's the model-facing deploy.
- Re-capture a bridge dump on a live goal session and confirm the prefix holds at a healthy cache_read baseline (DoD #3 empirical verify). Goal stays **active** until that lands.

The full src diff is shown above. **Approve the approach + the notice wording, and I'll clear the jiti cache and run the re-capture verification?** Or want changes to the notice text first?

Implementation complete and tested. Here's the critical-review checkpoint.

## Thinking-clear: bridge implementation (mirrors Claude Code v2.1.168 verbatim)

**Where:** `pi-claude-bridge/index.js` only — not the fork, not my-pi. The bridge is already the Claude Code emulation layer, so this is the faithful home and avoids a fork-core patch.

**What it does** (gated on the request actually carrying thinking, exactly like CC's `nY4`):
- Attaches body `context_management: { edits: [{ type: "clear_thinking_20251015", keep: "all" }] }`
- Appends beta `context-management-2025-06-27` to `anthropic-beta`
- Anthropic clears stale completed-turn thinking **server-side** and bills the reduced context
- Toggle: `BRIDGE_CLEAR_THINKING=off`

**Why it's cache-safe:** `context_management` is a top-level param (like `max_tokens`), not message content — it doesn't touch the cached prefix or the per-message fingerprints. Anthropic manages cache coherence around its own edits. No client-side surgery on signed blocks, so the 400 "latest assistant message cannot be modified" guard is never at risk.

**Tested:** 84 assertions green across the full suite. New Tests 11/12 assert the exact shape is injected when thinking is present and **absent** when it isn't.

**Diff is above** (`index.js` +43, `test-mock.js` +56). The `test-oauth-mode.js`/`scripts/cache-health.*` changes in that repo are the parallel session's, not mine.

## One honest caveat
The bridge re-sends all thinking each turn (Anthropic re-clears — idempotent, billed-reduced). That fixes the **billing + context** cost (your 400k problem). It does **not** shrink the on-wire payload or pi's local transcript — that needs the fork to consume the response's `context_management` field (what CC does to drop cleared blocks locally). Separate follow-up; not required for the win.

## Deploy
Going live = restarting `com.pi.claude-bridge` (pid 69886) — affects **every live pi session's** billing/behavior. That's your call. On your go I'll restart it, then capture a real opus dump and confirm (a) `context_management` is in the wire body and (b) the `usage` input tokens drop on a thinking-heavy request.

---
name: pi-thinking-clear
description: Why pi opus sessions balloon to 400k (thinking-block accumulation) and the bridge clear_thinking fix + its gate gotcha
metadata:
  type: project
---

On long opus-4.5+/sonnet-4.6+ pi sessions, accumulated extended-thinking blocks dominate the payload. Measured on a real burst dump (122 msgs, 163,307 tok): thinking **signatures alone = 81,983 tok (50.2%)**, thinking text+sig combined = 94,896 (58%) — bigger than all text + tool results + tool schemas combined.

Root: `pi-mono-fork/packages/ai/src/providers/anthropic.ts:1306-1331` round-trips every signed `thinking` block for every prior assistant turn (no latest-only gate). On **Opus 4.5+ / Sonnet 4.6+** Anthropic now *keeps and bills* previous-turn thinking (model-dependent; older models auto-strip). So the bloat is real billed context, re-billed on every deep cache bust, and accelerates compaction.

Fix shipped in **pi-claude-bridge/index.js** (NOT the fork — bridge is the Claude Code emulation layer), mirroring Claude Code v2.1.168 verbatim: when eligible, attach beta `context-management-2025-06-27` + body `context_management: { edits: [{ type: "clear_thinking_20251015", keep: "all" }] }` so Anthropic clears stale thinking server-side. Toggle `BRIDGE_CLEAR_THINKING=off`.

**Gate gotcha (caught by live test):** Anthropic 400s `"clear_thinking_20251015 strategy requires thinking to be enabled or adaptive"`. Gate on the top-level `params.thinking.type` being `enabled`/`adaptive` — NOT on thinking *blocks* being present. They diverge when thinking is toggled off mid-session (old blocks remain in history, `thinking` is disabled); gating on blocks would attach the edit and break the whole request. See `thinkingClearEligible`.

Follow-up (not done): bridge re-sends all thinking each turn (Anthropic re-clears, idempotent, billed-reduced) — fixes billing/context but not on-wire payload or pi's local transcript. Full shrink needs the **fork** to consume the response's `context_management` field and drop cleared blocks locally (what Claude Code does). Separate from the [[pi-goal-continuation-cache-bust]] root cause.

attachment.prompt: context_management? what is that?

content.text:
`context_management` is an Anthropic Messages API request field (gated behind the `context-management-2025-06-27` beta) — Anthropic's **"context editing"** feature. It lets you attach a declarative policy that Anthropic applies to the conversation **server-side, before processing and billing**.

How it works:
- You send the full conversation as normal, plus `context_management: { edits: [...] }`.
- Each entry in `edits` is a built-in pruning strategy. The two that exist:
  - `clear_thinking_20251015` — drop stale extended-thinking blocks from completed prior turns (what we're using)
  - `clear_tool_uses_20250919` — drop old tool-use/tool-result pairs
- Anthropic applies the edits, processes + **bills the reduced context**, and returns a `context_management` summary on the response telling you what it removed.

So it's server-managed context pruning. The value: the client keeps round-tripping everything (no risky surgery on the signed thinking blocks, which would trip the 400 guard), and Anthropic does the trimming and bills the smaller result. That's exactly why it beats a manual client-side strip — and it's how Claude Code keeps long sessions from ballooning.

What we inject:
```json
"context_management": { "edits": [{ "type": "clear_thinking_20251015", "keep": "all" }] }
```
= *"clear stale thinking from completed turns."* The `keep: "all"` is the exact value Claude Code's own client sends, so I mirrored it verbatim rather than guessing — its precise meaning I'd confirm from Anthropic's context-editing docs if you want certainty, but matching the reference client is the safe call.

---

**Where things stand** (both fixes live):

| Fix | Status |
|---|---|
| **pi-goal continuation cache-bust** (the original root cause) | Implemented, 412/412 tests, deployed (jiti cleared). Mechanism-verified by the byte-stability regression test. End-to-end dump confirms on the next pi *goal* session reload. |
| **Bridge thinking-clear** (the 400k amplifier) | Implemented, 13 mock tests, **deployed (bridge live, pid 59150)**, and **live-verified** — `context_management` injected on the real OAuth path, Anthropic accepts the shape, disabled-thinking correctly skipped. |
| DoD #4 cleanups | Verified already done (no `agent` in alwaysActive, dist current, ~140k comment fixed) |
| DoD #5 analyzer | `analyze-cache-breaks.mjs` extended with deep-message-bust classification |

Nothing committed (per your "push only when asked"). The bridge change is `index.js` + `test-mock.js` only — no fork patch. Want me to commit, or leave it in the working tree?

name: pi-thinking-clear
description: Why pi opus sessions balloon to 400k (thinking-block accumulation) and the bridge clear_thinking fix + its gate gotcha
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: d1d49ab5-cf53-4cc8-ba24-ee89badb820b
---

On long opus-4.5+/sonnet-4.6+ pi sessions, accumulated extended-thinking blocks dominate the payload. Measured on a real burst dump (122 msgs, 163,307 tok): thinking **signatures alone = 81,983 tok (50.2%)**, thinking text+sig combined = 94,896 (58%) — bigger than all text + tool results + tool schemas combined.

Root: `pi-mono-fork/packages/ai/src/providers/anthropic.ts:1306-1331` round-trips every signed `thinking` block for every prior assistant turn (no latest-only gate). On **Opus 4.5+ / Sonnet 4.6+** Anthropic now *keeps and bills* previous-turn thinking (model-dependent; older models auto-strip). So the bloat is real billed context, re-billed on every deep cache bust, and accelerates compaction.

Fix shipped in **pi-claude-bridge/index.js** (NOT the fork — bridge is the Claude Code emulation layer), mirroring Claude Code v2.1.168 verbatim: when eligible, attach beta `context-management-2025-06-27` + body `context_management: { edits: [{ type: "clear_thinking_20251015", keep: "all" }] }` so Anthropic clears stale thinking server-side. Toggle `BRIDGE_CLEAR_THINKING=off`.

**Gate gotcha (caught by live test):** Anthropic 400s `"clear_thinking_20251015 strategy requires thinking to be enabled or adaptive"`. Gate on the top-level `params.thinking.type` being `enabled`/`adaptive` — NOT on thinking *blocks* being present. They diverge when thinking is toggled off mid-session (old blocks remain in history, `thinking` is disabled); gating on blocks would attach the edit and break the whole request. See `thinkingClearEligible`.

Follow-up (not done): bridge re-sends all thinking each turn (Anthropic re-clears, idempotent, billed-reduced) — fixes billing/context but not on-wire payload or pi's local transcript. Full shrink needs the **fork** to consume the response's `context_management` field and drop cleared blocks locally (what Claude Code does). Separate from the [[pi-goal-continuation-cache-bust]] root cause.

  PASS: no context_management when request has no thinking blocks
  PASS: no context-management beta when request has no thinking

git commit -q -m "fix(pi-goal): byte-stable continuation supersession to stop cache bursts

Older pi_goal_continuation blocks were rewritten in place to a 'Superseded...'
stub when a newer continuation appended, mutating msg[K] deep in the message
history. On Anthropic's prompt cache that busts the cache from K to tail on every
continuation refresh (measured: DEEP-MESSAGE busts at msg[100], cache_read
174,878 -> 25,782 on a real goal session).

Stop mutating prior blocks. Supersession is now positional: the latest
continuation is authoritative by virtue of appearing last, and a
CONTINUATION_SUPERSEDE_NOTICE in every continuation builder tells the model to
act on the newest block only. Prior blocks stay byte-stable, so the cache prefix
survives each refresh.

Verified on a post-fix goal session (pi:goalverify-run1, 4 continuations):
0 DEEP-MESSAGE busts, 91% cache read (112,772 / 11,126). Tests flipped from
asserting the stub to asserting byte-stability; 412/412 pass." && git log --oneline -1

Now it's clear. The verified root cause, and a collision worth flagging:

## Root cause — verified, 0/3 adversarial lenses refuted it

**tool-search writes a live, *decreasing* counter into the cached prefix.** `tool-search/src/index.ts:557`:

```
<deferred-tools>
- ${entries.length} deferred tools available. Use tool_search(...) ...
</deferred-tools>
```

`entries.length` = tools not yet discovered. Every `tool_search` call shrinks it. `before_agent_start` re-injects the block into `params.system` **every turn** (`index.ts:324-327`). The bridge then moves all of `params.system` verbatim into `messages[0]` as `<system-context>` (`bridge/index.js:1583-1644`). So a count change = a byte change at **msg[0] position 0** = the entire conversation cache (up to 163 messages) re-billed.

The fingerprint signature matches exactly: `systemHash` stays stable (post-move it only sees `[billingBlock, ccPrefix]`), `perMessageHash[0]` changes → logged as *"messages mutated at position(s) 0"* — the **"other" bucket, 93.2% / 1,574 events**, the single biggest fleet-wide cache cost.

The irony: tool-search exists to *save* cache by deferring tool schemas — and it's the #1 cache-buster because it embeds a live counter in the prefix. Its own comment at `index.ts:299-302` even says *"Keep it deterministic and idempotent; prompt/schema churn here is a direct cache-prefix bust."* The count violates that. And it's a textbook breach of your standing directive: **no dynamic injection into the stable prompt boundary.**

**The fix is surgical** — make `renderDeferredBlock` byte-stable:
- Drop `${entries.length}` → static text (the model needs "deferred tools exist, use tool_search", not a live count).
- Derive the web hint from `s.catalog` (session-stable) instead of `stillDeferred` (turn-varying), so it doesn't flip when web tools get discovered.
- Result: identical bytes every turn → `injectOrReplaceBlock` is a no-op → zero msg[0] busts. Add a cache-stability test (render at count=50 vs count=3 → assert byte-identical).

**Collision flag:** `extensions/tool-search/src/index.ts` already has an *uncommitted* change from another session — it's the one that **added the `webHint`**, and that addition introduced the *second* variance (the hint flips present/absent as web tools get discovered). My fix lands in the same `renderDeferredBlock` function, so I'd be editing on top of foreign uncommitted work.

Secondary vectors (lower freq, not fixing now): pi-memory `injectedSection` cross-session bust (`pi-memory/index.ts:278,287`); bridge `hasConversationHistory` cache_control toggle on msg[0] (`bridge/index.js:1618`).

The <deferred-tools> hint embedded a live \"\${N} deferred tools available\" count
in the system prompt. tool-search re-injects this block every turn in
before_agent_start, and the claude bridge moves the whole system prompt verbatim
into messages[0] as <system-context> — the cached conversation prefix. Every
tool_search call shrank N, so the count changed turn-to-turn, mutating msg[0] and
busting the ENTIRE conversation cache from position 0. This was the single
biggest fleet-wide cache cost (the 'other'/prefix-anchor bucket: ~93% of bust
events; one byte at msg[0] re-bills the whole history, up to 160+ messages).

Ironically tool-search exists to SAVE cache via deferred schemas, and its own
comment warns 'prompt/schema churn here is a direct cache-prefix bust' — which
the count violated. It also breached the standing rule: no tool may dynamically
inject turn-varying content into the stable prompt boundary.

Fix: render the block purely from the session-stable catalog, never the shrinking
still-deferred subset. Drop the count (the model needs 'deferred tools exist, use
tool_search', not a live number). Derive the web hint from the full catalog
(stable all session, sorted for determinism) instead of the still-deferred set
(which flipped present/absent once web tools were activated). The block is now
byte-identical every turn → injectOrReplaceBlock no-ops → before_agent_start
returns undefined → zero msg[0] busts.

New test-deferred-block-stability.mjs locks the contract (no count,
order-independent, web hint session-stable, feature preserved). Smoke-test
assertions updated from the old per-turn-mutation contract to byte-stability.

The web-tools hint itself is the parallel session's in-progress feature, carried
here in a cache-safe form (it previously kept the count and added a second
variance). Gates: typecheck, stability test, smoke, test:extension-gate, live
prompt-health all green." && git log --oneline -1

---
name: pi-msg0-cache-bust
description: Why ANY turn-varying content in pi's params.system is a catastrophic msg[0] cache bust (bridge moves system→<system-context>), the fixed tool-search count, and the secondary vectors still open
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: d1d49ab5-cf53-4cc8-ba24-ee89badb820b
---

**Mental model — the #1 fleet-wide cache vector.** The claude bridge moves the WHOLE `params.system` verbatim into `messages[0]` as a `<system-context>` block (pi-claude-bridge/index.js ~1583-1644), then sets `params.system = [billingBlock, ccPrefix]`. So the system prompt IS the cached conversation prefix at position 0. Any byte that varies turn-to-turn in `params.system` — from ANY extension's `before_agent_start` — mutates msg[0] and busts the ENTIRE conversation cache from position 0 (logged as "messages mutated at position(s) 0" / "first divergence: msg[0] of N shared, N from tail"). This is the bridge's "other"/prefix-anchor bucket: ~93% of bust events, ~60% of all break-cost tokens. `systemHash` in cache-diagnostics.js stays stable (it only sees the post-move `[billingBlock, ccPrefix]`), so the bust shows ONLY in `perMessageHash[0]` — easy to misread as a message change rather than a system-prompt change.

**Diagnostic rule:** msg[0]-position busts with stable systemHash ⇒ something wrote turn-varying bytes into `params.system` before the bridge moved it. Audit every extension `before_agent_start` that returns `{ systemPrompt }`.

**Fixed (commit 5caec34):** tool-search's `<deferred-tools>` block embedded a live `${N} deferred tools available` count that shrank on every `tool_search` call → per-turn msg[0] bust. Now rendered from the session-stable catalog (no count; web hint derived from full catalog, sorted), byte-identical every turn. Guard: `extensions/tool-search/test-deferred-block-stability.mjs`. Reproduce/classify any future bust with `scripts/analyze-cache-breaks.mjs` against `~/.pi/agent/logs/claude-bridge.err.log`.

**Still open (secondary vectors, lower freq):**
- pi-memory `injectedSection` in the system prompt (extensions/pi-memory/index.ts ~278,287) — INJECT_MARKER-guarded so idempotent WITHIN a session, but the snapshot changes on dream consolidation ⇒ cross-session msg[0] bust in the same cwd.
- bridge `hasConversationHistory` toggling `cache_control` on msg[0]'s last block between turn 1 and turn 2+ (pi-claude-bridge/index.js ~1618) — changes the cache fingerprint even when content is byte-identical; secondary aggravator.

Related: [[pi-thinking-clear]] (the other big amplifier — accumulated thinking blocks). Same stack, different mechanism.

content.content:
# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## What This Is

A memory extension for the [pi coding agent](https://github.com/mariozechner/pi-mono). It provides persistent memory across coding sessions via plain markdown files, with optional semantic search powered by [qmd](https://github.com/tobi/qmd). Single-file extension (`index.ts`) — no build step, pi loads TypeScript directly.

## Commands

```bash
# Run e2e tests (requires `pi` on PATH with a configured API key)
bun test/e2e.ts

# Test the extension manually with pi
pi -p -e ./index.ts "remember: I prefer dark mode"

# Install into pi
pi install ./pi-memory
```

## Architecture

The entire extension is `index.ts` — a single default export function that receives pi's `ExtensionAPI` and:

1. **Registers lifecycle hooks**: `session_start` (detect qmd), `session_shutdown` (cleanup), `before_agent_start` (inject memory context into system prompt every turn), `session_before_compact` (warn about compaction)
2. **Registers 4 tools**: `memory_write`, `memory_read`, `scratchpad`, `memory_search`
3. **Manages files under `~/.pi/agent/memory/`**: `MEMORY.md` (long-term), `SCRATCHPAD.md` (checklist), `daily/<YYYY-MM-DD>.md` (append-only logs)

Key design patterns:
- Context injection via `before_agent_start` loads MEMORY.md + open scratchpad items + today/yesterday daily logs into the system prompt before every agent turn
- qmd integration is optional and detected at runtime — core tools work without it, only `memory_search` requires qmd
- After every write, a debounced (500ms) `qmd update` runs fire-and-forget in the background
- Scratchpad items are stored as markdown checklists with HTML comment metadata (`<!-- timestamp [sessionId] -->`)

## Peer Dependencies

Uses `@valkyriweb/pi-coding-agent` (ExtensionAPI types, Luke's `pi-mono-fork`), `@valkyriweb/pi-ai` (StringEnum), and `@sinclair/typebox` (schema definitions). These are peer deps — provided by the pi runtime. Upstream is `@mariozechner/*`; the fork republishes under `@earendil-works/*`.

## Testing

Tests are e2e only — they invoke `pi` as a subprocess with the extension loaded, send LLM prompts, and verify tool calls happened and files were written. Tests back up and restore `~/.pi/agent/memory/` files automatically. Each test runs a fresh `pi --no-session` invocation.

name: pi-msg0-cache-bust
description: Why ANY turn-varying content in pi's params.system is a catastrophic msg[0] cache bust (bridge moves system→<system-context>), the fixed tool-search count, and the secondary vectors still open
metadata:

**Mental model — the #1 fleet-wide cache vector.** The claude bridge moves the WHOLE `params.system` verbatim into `messages[0]` as a `<system-context>` block (pi-claude-bridge/index.js ~1583-1644), then sets `params.system = [billingBlock, ccPrefix]`. So the system prompt IS the cached conversation prefix at position 0. Any byte that varies turn-to-turn in `params.system` — from ANY extension's `before_agent_start` — mutates msg[0] and busts the ENTIRE conversation cache from position 0 (logged as "messages mutated at position(s) 0" / "first divergence: msg[0] of N shared, N from tail"). This is the bridge's "other"/prefix-anchor bucket: ~93% of bust events, ~60% of all break-cost tokens. `systemHash` in cache-diagnostics.js stays stable (it only sees the post-move `[billingBlock, ccPrefix]`), so the bust shows ONLY in `perMessageHash[0]` — easy to misread as a message change rather than a system-prompt change.

**Diagnostic rule:** msg[0]-position busts with stable systemHash ⇒ something wrote turn-varying bytes into `params.system` before the bridge moved it. Audit every extension `before_agent_start` that returns `{ systemPrompt }`.

**Fixed (commit 5caec34):** tool-search's `<deferred-tools>` block embedded a live `${N} deferred tools available` count that shrank on every `tool_search` call → per-turn msg[0] bust. Now rendered from the session-stable catalog (no count; web hint derived from full catalog, sorted), byte-identical every turn. Guard: `extensions/tool-search/test-deferred-block-stability.mjs`. Reproduce/classify any future bust with `scripts/analyze-cache-breaks.mjs` against `~/.pi/agent/logs/claude-bridge.err.log`.

- pi-memory `injectedSection` in the system prompt (extensions/pi-memory/index.ts ~278,287) — INJECT_MARKER-guarded so idempotent WITHIN a session, but the snapshot changes on dream consolidation ⇒ cross-session msg[0] bust in the same cwd.

Got the definitive topology. Here's the full report, then the closeout answer — which has a git snag worth catching.

---

# Session report — Pi cache-burst root causes

## The mission
Find and fix the real cause(s) of context/token "bursting" in Pi sessions. It turned out to be **four distinct root causes**, not one.

## Root causes fixed

| # | Vector | Root cause | Fix | Commit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **DEEP-MESSAGE bust** | pi-goal rewrote older continuation blocks in place to a "Superseded…" stub → mutated `msg[K]` deep in history → cache bust K→tail every refresh | Positional supersession: prior blocks stay byte-stable; a notice tells the model to act on the latest only | `3ddfe02` (my-pi) |
| 2 | **msg[0] / prefix-anchor** (the #1 vector, ~93% of bust events) | tool-search embedded a live `${N} deferred tools` count in the system prompt; the bridge moves `system`→`messages[0]`, so the shrinking count busted the *entire* cache from position 0 every `tool_search` call | Render the block from the session-stable catalog — no count, web hint sorted/catalog-derived — byte-identical every turn | `5caec34` (my-pi) |
| 3 | **400k thinking accumulation** | Anthropic signed-thinking blocks round-tripped + kept/billed every turn (Opus 4.5+/Sonnet 4.6+); inflates `cacheRead` → trips pi's compaction trigger | Bridge attaches `clear_thinking_20251015, keep:"all"` via the `context-management` beta — server strips thinking before KV-caching. Byte-identical to Claude Code's own `nY4` handler | `189374a` (bridge) |
| 4 | **`tools[]` bust on discovery** | The `Agent` tool can't be native-deferred (it shadows the core `agent` builtin), so discovering it loaded its full schema into `tools[]` | Made `Agent` eager via tool-search `alwaysActive` — stable schema, never bursts | `~/.pi/agent/settings.json` (runtime config, not a repo file) |

Plus tooling: `3523f48` (my-pi) — a cache-break classifier that buckets every bust by divergence position (tail-local / prefix-anchor / DEEP-MESSAGE), so the next burst is diagnosable.

## Ruled out — verified non-bugs (no change made)
Two "secondaries" I'd earlier flagged turned out not to be real on close inspection:
- **bridge `hasConversationHistory` `cache_control` toggle** — cache-content-neutral (`cache_control` is stripped before hashing; a marker toggle doesn't bust Anthropic's content-prefix read). It's a deliberate 4-marker-budget optimization.
- **pi-memory `injectedSection`** — idempotent per-turn (guarded), and lands in the dynamic system tail past the cache boundary cross-session. Doesn't bust the shared stable block.

I verified rather than mechanically patching load-bearing code — the tool-search count was the whole per-turn story.

## Verification / receipts
- **pi-goal:** 412/412 tests; real opus session showed **0 DEEP-MESSAGE busts, 91% cache read**.
- **tool-search msg[0]:** deterministic byte-stability test + **live receipt — a 2×`tool_search` session produced 0 prefix-anchor busts**.
- **thinking-clear:** confirmed working live — `cacheRead 419,731 → 46,364` once the clear fired on the real burst session.
- All gates green: `test:extension-gate`, bridge mock tests, typecheck, live prompt-health.

## The "are you sure?" check (you pushed, correctly)
I decomposed the actual 435k-token session and reverse-engineered the CC 2.1.168 binary:
- Thinking is the **#1 driver (~51%)** but **not** the 58% landslide I'd claimed — tool_results are a close ~49%, session-dependent. I corrected that overstatement.
- **Claude Code keeps all thinking on-wire AND in its transcript**, and relies entirely on the same server-side `clear_thinking`. So a fork-side trim would *diverge* from CC — **no fork change warranted**.

## Scope (so it's not misread later)
- **thinking-clear (400k):** Anthropic/**bridge-only** by design. Your `claude-bridge` is the only `anthropic-messages` provider, so all Claude traffic is covered; the fork applies no `context_management`, so a future direct `anthropic/*` provider would be the only gap. Codex reasoning/MLX don't have this failure mode.
- **tool-search & pi-goal fixes:** **provider-agnostic** (stable prefix / clean transcript help any provider's cache).
- **cache-break diagnostics:** bridge-only (only the bridge logs them).

## Memory updated
`pi-thinking-clear.md` (corrected figure + CC findings + scope), `pi-msg0-cache-bust.md` (created; secondaries marked ruled-out), `MEMORY.md` index.

## Optional / not done (recommend skip)
- Weighting thinking at ~0 in pi's local *estimate* path (`compaction.ts:265-266`, `tokenizer.ts:77-79`) — rarely fires (primary trigger anchors on post-strip usage) and diverges from CC.

## Ledger
4 commits, **none pushed** (as instructed): my-pi `3ddfe02` `3523f48` `5caec34`; bridge `189374a`. Plus the `settings.json` Agent edit. Parallel session's `commands.ts`/`recovery.ts` left untouched.

---

## Can you close out this session?

**Almost — but don't let the peer land its merge as-is.** Its status message has a stale view of `main`:

- The peer thinks `main` HEAD = `3523f48` and plans to **"fast-forward main to its verifier `24d1c65`."**
- **`main` is actually at `5caec34`** (my tool-search msg[0] fix, which landed *after* the peer's snapshot). I confirmed the topology:

```
3ddfe02 → 3523f48 ──┬── 5caec34   ← main HEAD (my msg[0] fix)
        (merge-base) └── 24d1c65   ← peer's verifier
```

They **diverged at `3523f48`**. So:

1. The peer's planned **fast-forward will fail** — `24d1c65` doesn't contain `5caec34`. An `--ff-only` will just refuse (no data loss), but it won't land.
2. ⚠️ **The risk:** if the peer "forces" the land (`git reset --hard 24d1c65` or `push -f`), it would **drop my `5caec34`** — the msg[0] fix. Tell it to **rebase `24d1c65` onto `5caec34`** instead (clean: disjoint files — verifier touches pi-goal `commands.ts`/`recovery.ts`, mine touches tool-search → no conflicts), then FF.
3. The peer also says the **msg[0] vector is "still open, no fix landed"** — that's **stale; it's fixed (`5caec34`)**. It doesn't need to pick that track up.

So: have the peer rebase onto `5caec34` (not reset to `24d1c65`), let its gate go green, FF main → then everything's on one clean linear history and you're safe to close out. Want me to do that rebase now, or leave it to the peer?

 What Factory Router is (your email)                                                                                          
                                                                                                                              
 Factory just shipped this on June 1. The pitch:                                                                              
 instead of expecting every engineer to always choose the best model manually, Factory Router automatically picks the best    
 model for each Droid session, drawing from a diverse pool of frontier and efficient models.                                  
 Their headline numbers:                                                                                                      
 on Terminal-Bench 2 it reached 99% of Opus 4.7's pass rate at 20% lower cost per session, and on Legacy-Bench it reached 96% 
 of the pass rate at 25% lower cost.                                                                                          
 The most honest part of their writeup is the cost curve — they admit aggressive routing has a cliff.                         
 Savings are easy when cheaper models take work they can already handle, then much harder once the router assigns difficult   
 work to models that cannot finish it; more aggressive routing would drop Terminal-Bench 2 performance to 81% of Opus at 56%  
 of the cost, and Legacy-Bench to 49% at 30% of the cost.                                                                     
 So the "20–25% savings at ~99% quality" is the conservative knee of the curve, not the maximum.                              
                                                                                                                              
 Beyond cost, it doubles as reliability infrastructure:                                                                       
 Droid sessions keep working when providers degrade or rate limits hit — Factory Router provides 99.9%+ request reliability   
 by routing across models, providers, and capacity sources, and if one provider path is unavailable it keeps sessions running 
 through another healthy path.                                                                                                
 Admins can also shape it:                                                                                                    
 you can give admin routing guidance so selection reflects how work actually happens — describing workflow patterns, codebase 
 areas, toolchains, and model preferences.                                                                                    
 It's currently private research preview, gated behind "ask for access."                                                      
                                                                                                                              
 The core idea                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                              
 The whole category rests on one observation:                                                                                 
 the price spread between frontier and smaller models is enormous and growing, and the key insight is that model capability   
 doesn't scale linearly with price — most queries don't need frontier capability.                                             
 A router classifies each request and sends simple work to a cheap model, hard work to a frontier model.                      
 Done well, routing cuts LLM costs by 50–85% with minimal quality degradation; done poorly, it creates silent quality         
 regressions you won't detect until users churn.                                                                              
 That "silent regression" risk is the recurring warning across every source — the same one Factory flags about its own cliff. 
                                                                                                                              
 Who's doing it — the landscape                                                                                               
                                                                                                                              
 Research / open foundations:                                                                                                 
 - RouteLLM (LMSYS, the Chatbot Arena team) — the academic reference.                                                         
 Trained routers reduce costs by up to 85% while maintaining 95% GPT-4 performance on MT Bench, and achieve the same          
 performance as commercial offerings while being >40% cheaper.                                                                
 It's a 2-model framework (strong vs. weak) with a tunable cost threshold.                                                    
                                                                                                                              
 Hyperscaler / platform:                                                                                                      
 - Microsoft Foundry Model Router —                                                                                           
 a purpose-built ML model trained on hundreds of thousands of examples that routes prompts in real time to the best-suited    
 LLM, optimizing for quality, cost, and latency.                                                                              
 It exposes three modes:                                                                                                      
 Balanced (default, optimizes cost while maintaining quality), Quality (critical reasoning tasks), and Cost (high-volume      
 budget-sensitive workloads).                                                                                                 
 Commercial routers:                                                                                                          
 - OpenRouter — mostly an aggregation gateway (400+ models), but its Auto Router is a real router:                            
 powered by NotDiamond, it analyzes your prompt and selects from a curated pool, and you pay the standard rate for whichever  
 model is selected with no additional routing fee.                                                                            
 Important nuance:                                                                                                            
 it optimizes for output quality, picking the best model for each prompt — it does not optimize for cost by routing simple    
 prompts to cheaper tiers.                                                                                                    
 The market treats it as infrastructure now —                                                                                 
 OpenRouter's recent $113M Series B and its claim that weekly volume grew from 5 trillion to 25 trillion tokens in six months 
 show the broader market is already treating model routing as infrastructure.                                                 
 - NotDiamond, Martian, Unify, Requesty, ShareAI — the dedicated commercial players.                                          
 Routers like CARROT and GraphRouter illustrate cost-efficient routing, while systems such as GPT-5 and NotDiamond lean       
 heavily on expensive models for accuracy.                                                                                    
 - LiteLLM — worth separating out because it's frequently miscategorized:                                                     
 LiteLLM is primarily a proxy, not a router — it doesn't include intelligent task classification, you still choose which      
 model to call, and routing logic must be built on top.                                                                       
 How routers actually decide                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                              
 Several strategies, roughly in order of sophistication:                                                                      
 Rule-based routing uses predefined logic; similarity-based routing compares the request to past queries using embeddings;    
 machine-learning routing trains a classifier on historical data.                                                             
 - Cascading —                                                                                                                
 progressive escalation through model tiers, starting cheap and escalating only when needed.                                  
 - The classifier approach is what most production systems use, and the RouteLLM result is the canonical proof point:         
 routing can achieve 95% of GPT-4's performance while using GPT-4 for only 14% of queries on GSM8K.                           
 One important architectural note for agentic/coding work specifically (which is Factory's whole focus):                      
 for multi-step agent workflows, routing extends beyond the entry point — each tool call, sub-task, and reasoning step can be 
 dispatched to the appropriate specialist, with a lightweight orchestrator acting as a dispatcher. This is where routing      
 evolves from a cost optimization into an architectural pattern.                                                              
 The catch everyone names                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                              
 The consistent caution: routing is invisible until it fails.                                                                 
 The risk is that routing becomes invisible until something goes wrong — if an agent fails because it was sent to the wrong   
 model, the savings will not feel like savings.                                                                               
 And the genuinely hard judgment a good router makes isn't "what's cheapest" —                                                
 a good router does not merely pick the cheapest model; it decides when cost savings are harmless and when they become        
 expensive because the weaker model fails, retries, or sends the task back to a human.                                        
 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

 routing) doing per-task model selection, plus the claude-bridge layer that all Anthropic calls flow through — which is       
 structurally the same "gateway + routing decision" architecture these products sell. The interesting angle for you isn't     
 adopting Factory (it's a closed Droid-only preview), but whether the published cost-curve methodology — measuring cost per

# Pi Development — Router

## Core rule

- Customize Pi via `~/Projects/personal/my-pi` extensions/packages first.
- Patch `~/Projects/personal/pi-mono-fork` core only for generic platform primitives that cannot be exposed through existing hooks/filters.
- If core changes are unavoidable, log them in `my-pi/docs/pi-fork-patch-inventory.md` and run the fork + extension gates.

## Read when

| Work | Read |
|---|---|
| Any Pi extension/package/fork implementation | `~/Projects/agent-scripts/references/pi-dev-details.md` |
| Prompt-cache, `tools[]`, system prompt, `forkAgent`, child agents, memory extractors | skill `pi-cache-stability` + `my-pi/docs/cache-strategy.md` |
| Extension API / examples | `~/Projects/personal/pi-mono-fork/packages/coding-agent/docs/extensions.md` |
| Runtime/package inventory | `~/Projects/personal/my-pi/docs/pi-stack-inventory.md` |
| Setup/runtime registry changes | `~/Projects/personal/my-pi/docs/pi-setup/` catalog YAML; generated files are scanner-owned |
| Config settings / env layering | `~/Projects/personal/my-pi/docs/config-layering.md` |
| Release/versioning/rollback | `~/Projects/personal/my-pi/docs/release-engineering.md` |

## Hot paths

- Core fork: `~/Projects/personal/pi-mono-fork` (`packages/coding-agent` for agent loop/tools/docs).
- Extension lab: `~/Projects/personal/my-pi/extensions/`.
- Full profile: `~/Projects/personal/my-pi/packages/my-pi-full/package.json`.
- Claude bridge: `~/Projects/personal/pi-claude-bridge` at `http://127.0.0.1:9100`.
- Model metadata: `~/.pi/agent/models.json`; Opus 4.8 is `claude-bridge/claude-opus-4-8`.

## Cache footguns

- Keep `params.system` and `tools[]` byte-stable across same-cwd sessions.
- Put dynamic recall/time/status/session data in appended messages/tool results, not cached system-prefix text.
- Mark situational/heavy extension tools `deferLoading: true`; gate with `npm --prefix ~/Projects/personal/my-pi run check:deferred-tool-contracts`.
- Guard `setActiveTools`: call only when the normalized tool-name set changes.
- Prefer `tool_reference` / provider-native `defer_loading` over mutating active tools after `tool_search`.

## Gates

- Extension/profile/cache surface: `npm --prefix ~/Projects/personal/my-pi run test:extension-gate`.
- Fork/core surface: `npm --prefix ~/Projects/personal/pi-mono-fork run test:build-gate`.
- Native aliases: `node ~/Projects/personal/my-pi/extensions/native-tool-overrides/test-load.mjs`.
- Prompt-health probe: `pi-prompt-health --refresh`, send one Pi message, then `pi-prompt-health`.

# How I Work

Use progressive disclosure where possible for context efficiency, see progressive-disclosure skill

Tradeoff: These guidelines bias toward caution over speed. For trivial tasks, use judgment.

1. Think Before Coding
Don't assume. Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs.

Before implementing:

State your assumptions explicitly. If uncertain, ask.
If multiple interpretations exist, present them - don't pick silently.
If a simpler approach exists, say so. Push back when warranted.
If something is unclear, stop. Name what's confusing. Ask.
2. Simplicity First
Minimum code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative.

Good code should read like a clear action sequence:

```ts
const harness = await init({ model });
const session = await harness.session();
const result = await session.prompt(prompt, { schema });
```

```php
Route::resource('photos', PhotoController::class)
    ->only(['index', 'show']);

Flight::where('active', 1)
    ->orderBy('name')
    ->limit(10)
    ->get();
```

No features beyond what was asked.
No abstractions for single-use code.
No "flexibility" or "configurability" that wasn't requested.
No error handling for impossible scenarios.
If you write 200 lines and it could be 50, rewrite it.
Ask yourself: "Would a senior engineer say this is overcomplicated?" If yes, simplify.

3. Surgical Changes
Touch only what you must. Quality improvements stay inside the task's boundary.

Reuse before adding:

Reuse existing types, utilities, hooks, components, and patterns before writing new ones.
Don't broaden public APIs unless the acceptance criteria require it.

When editing existing code:

Don't "improve" adjacent code, comments, or formatting.
Don't refactor things that aren't broken.
Match existing style, even if you'd do it differently.
If you notice unrelated dead code, mention it - don't delete it.

When quality blocks the task:

If confusing, duplicated, or hard-to-test code blocks a clean implementation, improve that code as part of the change.
If a small local cleanup makes the implementation simpler or safer, do it and call it out (PR body / summary).
A real quality issue not needed for the change → flag it for follow-up; don't expand scope.

When your changes create orphans:
Remove imports/variables/functions that YOUR changes made unused.
Don't remove pre-existing dead code unless asked.
The test: Every changed line should trace directly to the user's request.

4. Goal-Driven Execution
Define success criteria. Loop until verified.

Transform tasks into verifiable goals:

"Add validation" → "Write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass"
"Fix the bug" → "Write a test that reproduces it, then make it pass"
"Refactor X" → "Ensure tests pass before and after"
For multi-step tasks, state a brief plan:

1. [Step] → verify: [check]
2. [Step] → verify: [check]
3. [Step] → verify: [check]
Strong success criteria let you loop independently. Weak criteria ("make it work") require constant clarification.

For spec-backed work:
- Keep each slice traceable to a spec section, issue, or acceptance bullet.
- Answer "what's left?" with concrete file/task deltas, not broad themes.
- After risky or architecture-heavy slices, report done, yet-to-do, spec deviations, roadblocks, and harder-than-expected parts.
- Treat review feedback as a loop: implement slice → inspect diff/comments → fix → promote repeated style feedback into AGENTS.md or the relevant skill.
- Checkpoint completed slices before starting a risky refactor.
- For gnarly threads, write a short handoff that links existing specs/artifacts instead of duplicating them.

These guidelines are working if: fewer unnecessary changes in diffs, fewer rewrites due to overcomplication, and clarifying questions come before implementation rather than after mistakes.

Don’t fight errors: after the same error twice, stop and gather new evidence — local docs/source first, then web if version/API behavior is unclear — before choosing a fix.

# IDENTITY.md — Rusty

- **Name:** Rusty
- **Emoji:** 🦊
- **Role:** Luke's daily-driver dev agent.
- **Range:** Pi, Claude Code, Codex, local shells, remote machines.
- **Job:** Luke's right hand man, improve work, Ship code, fix broken things, explain the weird bits, automate boring work, and keep momentum.
- **Avatar:** none yet. Use a path relative to `~/Projects/agent-scripts/`, an `https://` URL, or a `data:` URI.

# SOUL.md — Rusty

## Core

**Just answer.** Never open with "Great question", "I'd be happy to help", or "Absolutely". Just answer.

**Brevity is mandatory.** If the answer fits in one sentence, one sentence is what Luke gets. Long replies are a tax; charge only when worth it.

**Have opinions. Strong ones.** Stop hiding behind "it depends". Pick the best path, say why, move.

**Do the obvious work.** Reversible, local, boring? Do it. Ask only for destructive, external, private, or genuinely ambiguous moves.

**Use tools before asking.** Read the file. Check the log. Grep the repo. Come back with answers, not vibes.

**Call out bad ideas early.** If Luke is about to footgun himself, say so. Charm over cruelty, but don't sugarcoat.

**Keep private private.** Don't leak Luke's stuff. Don't act as Luke in public without a clear go-ahead. No PII in github.

## Voice

- Sharp, warm, terse.
- Opinionated without being a dick.
- Funny when it happens naturally. No forced jokes.
- Swearing is allowed when it lands. A real "holy shit" beats five sterile adjectives. Don't overdo it.
- Telegraph style. Drop filler. Match Luke's pace.
- Praise only when earned. If something is fucking brilliant, say so.

## Vibe

Smart friend at the desk. Calm under pressure. Dry wit. Clean takes. No corporate mist. No sycophant sludge.

Be the assistant you'd actually want to talk to at 2am. Not a corporate drone. Not a sycophant. Just... good.

## Continuity

These files are memory. Read them. Update them when Luke asks or when a real preference becomes obvious.

If you change this file, tell Luke.

When to reach for it:
  · Building anything that benefits from MULTIPLE specialized roles working in parallel — designer + developer + reviewer, researcher + writer + fact-checker, planner + executor + critic.

  · Anywhere you would otherwise spawn the Task tool repeatedly for sub-tasks — prefer AgenticMail when those sub-tasks need to talk to EACH OTHER, not just back to you.

High-leverage tools:
  · mcp__agenticmail__create_account({ name, role })       — spawn a fresh persistent agent identity with its own inbox + API key.

  · mcp__agenticmail__call_agent({ agent, message }) / mcp__agenticmail__wait_for_email — blocking RPC when you need a specific answer back before continuing your own turn.

Coordination pattern: one email thread = the shared workspace. Reply-all keeps the audit trail. Use `wake` to control whose turn it is.

Other tools cover: inbox/folder management, drafts, templates, tasks, contacts, signatures, SMS, voice. Full list under mcp__agenticmail__* — discover on demand, don't front-load them all.

 Thinking...                                                                                                                  

 I've got a solid picture from the research. Here's what's going on with model routing — starting with the Factory Router     
 that triggered your email, then the broader landscape.                                                                       
                                                                                                                              
 What Factory Router is (your email)                                                                                          
                                                                                                                              
 Factory just shipped this on June 1. The pitch:                                                                              
 instead of expecting every engineer to always choose the best model manually, Factory Router automatically picks the best    
 model for each Droid session, drawing from a diverse pool of frontier and efficient models.                                  
 Their headline numbers:                                                                                                      
 on Terminal-Bench 2 it reached 99% of Opus 4.7's pass rate at 20% lower cost per session, and on Legacy-Bench it reached 96% 
 of the pass rate at 25% lower cost.                                                                                          
 The most honest part of their writeup is the cost curve — they admit aggressive routing has a cliff.                         
 Savings are easy when cheaper models take work they can already handle, then much harder once the router assigns difficult   
 work to models that cannot finish it; more aggressive routing would drop Terminal-Bench 2 performance to 81% of Opus at 56%  
 of the cost, and Legacy-Bench to 49% at 30% of the cost.                                                                     
 So the "20–25% savings at ~99% quality" is the conservative knee of the curve, not the maximum.                              
                                                                                                                              
 Beyond cost, it doubles as reliability infrastructure:                                                                       
 Droid sessions keep working when providers degrade or rate limits hit — Factory Router provides 99.9%+ request reliability   
 by routing across models, providers, and capacity sources, and if one provider path is unavailable it keeps sessions running 
 through another healthy path.                                                                                                
 Admins can also shape it:                                                                                                    
 you can give admin routing guidance so selection reflects how work actually happens — describing workflow patterns, codebase 
 areas, toolchains, and model preferences.                                                                                    
 It's currently private research preview, gated behind "ask for access."                                                      
                                                                                                                              
 The core idea                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                              
 The whole category rests on one observation:                                                                                 
 the price spread between frontier and smaller models is enormous and growing, and the key insight is that model capability   
 doesn't scale linearly with price — most queries don't need frontier capability.                                             
 A router classifies each request and sends simple work to a cheap model, hard work to a frontier model.                      
 Done well, routing cuts LLM costs by 50–85% with minimal quality degradation; done poorly, it creates silent quality         
 regressions you won't detect until users churn.                                                                              
 That "silent regression" risk is the recurring warning across every source — the same one Factory flags about its own cliff. 
                                                                                                                              
 Who's doing it — the landscape                                                                                               
                                                                                                                              
 Research / open foundations:                                                                                                 
 - RouteLLM (LMSYS, the Chatbot Arena team) — the academic reference.                                                         
 Trained routers reduce costs by up to 85% while maintaining 95% GPT-4 performance on MT Bench, and achieve the same          
 performance as commercial offerings while being >40% cheaper.                                                                
 It's a 2-model framework (strong vs. weak) with a tunable cost threshold.                                                    
                                                                                                                              
 Hyperscaler / platform:                                                                                                      
 - Microsoft Foundry Model Router —                                                                                           
 a purpose-built ML model trained on hundreds of thousands of examples that routes prompts in real time to the best-suited    
 LLM, optimizing for quality, cost, and latency.                                                                              
 It exposes three modes:                                                                                                      
 Balanced (default, optimizes cost while maintaining quality), Quality (critical reasoning tasks), and Cost (high-volume      
 budget-sensitive workloads).                                                                                                 
 Commercial routers:                                                                                                          
 - OpenRouter — mostly an aggregation gateway (400+ models), but its Auto Router is a real router:                            
 powered by NotDiamond, it analyzes your prompt and selects from a curated pool, and you pay the standard rate for whichever  
 model is selected with no additional routing fee.                                                                            
 Important nuance:                                                                                                            
 it optimizes for output quality, picking the best model for each prompt — it does not optimize for cost by routing simple    
 prompts to cheaper tiers.                                                                                                    
 The market treats it as infrastructure now —                                                                                 
 OpenRouter's recent $113M Series B and its claim that weekly volume grew from 5 trillion to 25 trillion tokens in six months 
 show the broader market is already treating model routing as infrastructure.                                                 
 - NotDiamond, Martian, Unify, Requesty, ShareAI — the dedicated commercial players.                                          
 Routers like CARROT and GraphRouter illustrate cost-efficient routing, while systems such as GPT-5 and NotDiamond lean       
 heavily on expensive models for accuracy.                                                                                    
 - LiteLLM — worth separating out because it's frequently miscategorized:                                                     
 LiteLLM is primarily a proxy, not a router — it doesn't include intelligent task classification, you still choose which      
 model to call, and routing logic must be built on top.                                                                       
 How routers actually decide                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                              
 Several strategies, roughly in order of sophistication:                                                                      
 Rule-based routing uses predefined logic; similarity-based routing compares the request to past queries using embeddings;    
 machine-learning routing trains a classifier on historical data.                                                             
 - Cascading —                                                                                                                
 progressive escalation through model tiers, starting cheap and escalating only when needed.                                  
 - The classifier approach is what most production systems use, and the RouteLLM result is the canonical proof point:         
 routing can achieve 95% of GPT-4's performance while using GPT-4 for only 14% of queries on GSM8K.                           
 One important architectural note for agentic/coding work specifically (which is Factory's whole focus):                      
 for multi-step agent workflows, routing extends beyond the entry point — each tool call, sub-task, and reasoning step can be 
 dispatched to the appropriate specialist, with a lightweight orchestrator acting as a dispatcher. This is where routing      
 evolves from a cost optimization into an architectural pattern.                                                              
 The catch everyone names                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                              
 The consistent caution: routing is invisible until it fails.                                                                 
 The risk is that routing becomes invisible until something goes wrong — if an agent fails because it was sent to the wrong   
 model, the savings will not feel like savings.                                                                               
 And the genuinely hard judgment a good router makes isn't "what's cheapest" —                                                
 a good router does not merely pick the cheapest model; it decides when cost savings are harmless and when they become        
 expensive because the weaker model fails, retries, or sends the task back to a human.

Not a merge or build problem — it's a **process-restart** problem. Your running session is executing stale code from memory.

Here's the evidence:

**The fixes are all landed and live-on-disk:**
- `5caec34` (tool-search byte-stable block) — **in main's ancestry**, main now at `546f240`.
- tool-search loads from `src/index.ts` directly via jiti (`main: "src/index.ts"`, registered as `../../extensions/tool-search/src/index.ts`). **No build step exists or is needed** — the committed source *is* the runtime.
- Bridge `clear_thinking` (`189374a`, committed 13:33) — running bridge pid 72795 **started 18:11**, so it already has it. ✓

**But pi loads each extension once, at process startup.** Your running sessions:

| pi PID | started | vs fix (14:19) |
|---|---|---|
| 60370 | **10:11** | ⚠️ stale |
| 89727 | **11:30** | ⚠️ stale |
| 17125 | 16:01 | ✓ current |
| 27102+ | 21:30+ | ✓ current |

If the session you're hitting issues in is one of the morning ones (10:11 / 11:30), it's still running the *old* tool-search module with the live `${count}` cache-bust baked in — the jiti module is cached in that process's memory and a git commit can't reach into it.

**Fix: restart that pi session.** No rebuild, no reinstall — just exit and relaunch `pi`. The new process reads `src/index.ts` at startup and you're on the byte-stable block.

One caveat worth naming: even after restart, the *first* turn of a fresh session always shows a big cache-write (it's establishing the prefix). The win shows up turn-2 onward — `R` (cache read) should dominate and you shouldn't see prefix-anchor busts when tool_search fires. If you restart and *still* see bursting on later turns, that's a genuinely new signal and worth digging into — but I'd bet a fresh session clears it.
